recent_posts.title: WCAG3 Contrast as of April 2026
recent_posts.summary: APCA contrast was removed from WCAG3 working drafts in 2023 and the current WCAG3 spec explicitly states the contrast algorithm is yet to be determined. Despite this, many tools and teams continue to promote APCA as the definitive WCAG3 contrast method, which creates legal risk for those who abandon WCAG2 contrast requirements based on that advice. WCAG3 is unlikely to be finalized before 2030. Until then, developers should either ensure colors also pass WCAG2 contrast requirements, or carefully document any deviations with legal counsel.

recent_posts.title: Accessibility Law of Headlines
recent_posts.summary: A proposed amendment to Betteridge's law of headlines for the digital accessibility space: any headline asserting something is accessible is wrong. The post argues that absolute accessibility claims are inherently false, since you can't make something accessible to everyone. It also warns that many such claims come from corporate marketing designed to sell accessibility products rather than genuinely help users, linking to a long list of prior posts debunking specific tools and vendors.

recent_posts.title: Your Browser Can Already Speak a Page
recent_posts.summary: Browsers already have built-in text-to-speech features that let users listen to web pages at no cost — Firefox, Chrome, Edge, and Safari all support this natively. Third-party vendors, AI companies, and accessibility overlay providers pitching paid read-aloud solutions are largely unnecessary, and often come with downsides: environmental cost from AI processing, legal risk from overlays, user tracking, and unreliable functionality. Users who genuinely rely on spoken content typically already know about and prefer browser-native or extension-based tools. The only caveat is that these browser features work best on well-structured HTML, so if they don't work on your site, that's a signal to fix your markup.

recent_posts.title: Honoring Mobile OS Text Size
recent_posts.summary: Mobile browsers handle OS-level text size settings differently. Firefox automatically scales web text with Android system settings. Safari requires specific CSS using `-apple-system-body` font properties. Chrome is introducing a new `<meta name="text-scale" content="scale">` tag that requires authors to avoid fixed font sizes and use relative units. A combined approach using both the meta tag and Safari's CSS can enable text scaling across all three rendering engines, improving accessibility for users who adjust system font sizes.

recent_posts.title: Don't split words into letters for animations or styling
recent_posts.summary: GSAP's SplitText plugin claims screen reader support but fails across most screen reader/browser combinations. Splitting words into individual letters wrapped in HTML elements creates accessibility barriers, even when using aria-label and aria-hidden. Testing across NVDA, JAWS, Narrator, VoiceOver, Orca, and TalkBack reveals only NVDA/Firefox and TalkBack/Chrome work correctly. The generic role on divs prohibits aria-label, and even when used on valid elements, aria-label doesn't translate and can violate WCAG Label in Name requirements. Developers should avoid splitting text into letters for animations or styling effects.

recent_posts.title: Barriers from Links with ARIA
recent_posts.summary: Testing reveals that using aria-label on links, aria-hidden within links, and splitting letters across span elements creates barriers beyond screen readers. Browser text-to-speech features (Edge Read Aloud, Chrome reader mode, Safari Speech) fail to announce aria-label values, skip aria-hidden content entirely, and struggle with letter-separated text. Chrome's reader mode even visually hides aria-hidden links. The key recommendations: avoid aria-label on links, don't use aria-hidden within links, and don't split words across elements.

recent_posts.title: Live Region Support
recent_posts.summary: Comprehensive testing results for ARIA live regions across major screen readers (NVDA, JAWS, Narrator, VoiceOver, Orca, TalkBack) reveal inconsistent behavior. The analysis covers five live region types: polite, assertive, alert role, HTML output element, and dynamic aria-describedby. Key findings show that polite/assertive distinctions are often ignored, alert roles rarely announce "alert" prefix, and support varies significantly between audio and Braille output. All tested screen readers correctly hide regions marked as hidden. Includes detailed version-specific results and a testing demo with multiple hiding methods.

recent_posts.title: Brief Note on Application Keyboard Shortcuts
recent_posts.summary: Screen readers include pass-through commands that allow users to bypass screen reader key bindings and send keystrokes directly to applications. NVDA, JAWS, Narrator, Orca, and VoiceOver each have specific commands for this functionality. Developers shouldn't avoid certain keyboard shortcuts due to screen reader conflicts, but should document pass-through commands for users and inform QA teams to prevent unnecessary bug reports.

recent_posts.title: My Use of ‘AI’ on this Site
recent_posts.summary: A web accessibility expert discloses their past use of AI-generated images on their blog and commits to discontinuing the practice, citing ethical concerns about content theft. They pledge never to use LLMs for writing content, list all instances where AI-generated images appeared in their posts since 2022, and outline their personal policy of blocking sites that use LLM-generated content. The author maintains their blog will remain human-written and won't focus on AI topics.

recent_posts.title: Accessibility is about continuous improvement, not universal perfection
recent_posts.summary: Accessibility is fundamentally about people, not just technical compliance. WCAG conformance (even at AAA level) doesn't guarantee universal accessibility due to varying user needs, contexts, technologies, and abilities. Rather than claiming something is universally accessible, practitioners should specify what accessibility features are implemented. The goal is continuous improvement to serve more people, acknowledging that perfect accessibility for everyone is unattainable given human diversity and technological limitations.

top_posts.title: Be Careful Using ‘Grid’
top_posts.summary: The term 'grid' in web development can refer to various patterns, and it's crucial to be specific about which one is being used. These include CSS Grid, CSS Subgrid, ARIA Grid, ARIA Treegrid, HTML Tables, and Data Grids, each serving different purposes from layout design to creating interactive elements. Misusing these terms can lead to confusion and accessibility issues.

top_posts.title: OpenAI's misguided ARIA recommendations threaten web accessibility and enable SEO abuse
top_posts.summary: OpenAI's new Atlas browser encourages website owners to add ARIA tags to improve ChatGPT agent compatibility, but this recommendation reveals fundamental misunderstandings of ARIA's purpose and accessibility principles. The guidance could incentivize SEO practitioners to misuse ARIA attributes through keyword stuffing, similar to historical alt text abuse, potentially making websites less accessible while enabling content scraping. OpenAI has a documented three-year history of accessibility failures in its own products, yet now positions ARIA as metadata for bot navigation rather than its intended purpose as assistive technology support.

top_posts.title: Accesstive accessibility overlay review reveals serious flaws and questionable claims
top_posts.summary: Adrian Roselli analyzes Accesstive's accessibility overlay product and finds significant issues including WCAG violations, non-functional features for screen readers, and questionable marketing claims. The review reveals that the overlay introduces more accessibility problems than it solves, with fake testimonials and case studies from non-existent companies. Roselli demonstrates through testing that basic overlay functions fail to work properly and argues that accessibility overlays generally increase legal risk rather than providing protection.
